findings.issue_text: `packages/app-store/_utils/oauth/parseRefreshTokenResponse.ts:29` returns `refreshTokenResponse` (a `SafeParseSuccess`, i.e. `{ success: true, data: {...} }`) instead of `refreshTokenResponse.data`. At `packages/app-store/googlecalendar/lib/CalendarService.ts:97-100` that value is written straight to the DB as `data: { key }`.

`packages/app-store/salesforce/lib/CalendarService.ts:96` calls `await prisma.credential.update(...)`, but the import block (lines 1-20) has no `import prisma from "@calcom/prisma"`. This is a hard `tsc` failure, and at runtime the Salesforce integration is dead on arrival: the refresh runs inside `getClient`, which is called from the constructor, so *every* Salesforce operation throws. Add the import.

`packages/app-store/_utils/oauth/createOAuthAppCredential.ts:30-56`. The `state?.teamId` branch only verifies the caller is an *accepted member* of the team, then creates the team-wide credential and returns. `throwIfNotHaveAdminAccessToTeam` is called at line 59 — after the early return — so it only ever runs with `teamId: null`, where it is a no-op.

`packages/app-store/_utils/oauth/refreshOAuthTokens.ts:8-15` POSTs `{calcomUserId, appSlug}` to `CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT` with no headers at all. `CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET` / `CALCOM_WEBHOOK_HEADER_NAME` are only checked on the *inbound* webhook.

`apps/web/pages/api/webhook/app-credential.ts:40-54` selects `{ slug: true }` and indexes `appStoreMetadata[app.slug]`. `appStoreMetadata` is keyed by app *directory name*, which differs from the slug for exactly the apps this feature targets: slug `google-calendar` → dir `googlecalendar`, `office365-calendar` → `office365calendar`, `msteams` → `office365video`, `lark-calendar` → `larkcalendar`.

`packages/app-store/salesforce/lib/CalendarService.ts:75-107`. The refresh is unconditional — no expiry check, unlike every other integration — so a token round-trip to `login.salesforce.com` happens on each `new SalesforceCalendarService(...)`. Worse, the freshly-issued token is persisted to the DB but the returned `jsforce.Connection` (line 101) is still built from the stale `credentialKey.access_token` and `credentialKey.instance_url`. So the extra call buys nothing and an expired credential stays expired for the current request. Gate on expiry, and build the connection from `accessTokenParsed.data`.

`packages/app-store/salesforce/lib/CalendarService.ts:86`. `statusText` is an empty string over HTTP/2 and for any non-standard reason phrase, so healthy responses throw `HttpError` with an empty message. Use `if (!response.ok)`.

`packages/app-store/_utils/oauth/parseRefreshTokenResponse.ts:5-11`. `z.string().toString()` is `"[object Object]"`, and the second computed key overwrites the first, so the schema is effectively `z.object({ access_token: z.string(), "[object Object]": z.unknown().optional() })`. The commented intent ("any property with a number is the expiry", "allow other properties") is not implemented, and because zod strips unknown keys by default, **every field except `access_token` is discarded**.

`parseRefreshTokenResponse.ts:25-27` sets `data.refresh_token = "refresh_token"` whenever the field is falsy, regardless of which schema branch ran. Office 365's `refreshTokenResponseSchema:56` declares `refresh_token` optional, and line 264 spreads the result over the stored credential — so any Microsoft response that omits `refresh_token` overwrites the real one with the literal string `"refresh_token"`, unrecoverably. Only apply the placeholder inside the credential-sharing branch.

`webex/lib/VideoApiAdapter.ts:87` validates with `webexRefreshedTokenSchema`, which requires `scope: z.literal("spark:kms ...")`, `token_type: z.literal("Bearer")` and `refresh_token_expires_in` → always rejects.
`larkcalendar/lib/CalendarService.ts:83` calls `handleLarkError`, which expects Lark's `{code, data:{...}}` envelope → always rejects.
`hubspot/lib/CalendarService.ts:177` types the result as `HubspotToken` and reads `.expiresIn` off a `Response` → `expiryDate: NaN`, `setAccessToken(undefined)`, swallowed by the surrounding `catch`.
`googlecalendar/lib/CalendarService.ts:94` reads `res?.data` off a `Response` → `undefined`, then `token.access_token` throws.

`apps/web/pages/api/webhook/app-credential.ts:17,31,57-59`. A `GET` reaches `schema.parse(undefined)`; a malformed body, a wrong encryption key, or non-JSON plaintext throws out of `symmetricDecrypt`/`JSON.parse`. All of these surface as unhandled 500s (with stack traces in non-production) rather than 400s. Add a method guard and wrap parse/decrypt in `safeParse` + `try/catch` returning 400.

`apps/web/pages/api/webhook/app-credential.ts:73-80` writes only `key`. Cal.com marks credentials `invalid: true` on `invalid_grant` (see `googlecalendar/lib/CalendarService.ts:108-113`), and invalid credentials are filtered out of calendar lookups. So the sync push that is supposed to *repair* a broken credential leaves it disabled. Add `invalid: false` to the update payload.

`apps/web/pages/api/webhook/app-credential.ts:62-70` uses `findFirst` on `(userId, appId)` with no ordering. A user with two Google Calendar accounts gets one of them overwritten at random with the other's keys. The comment ("Can't use prisma upsert as we don't know the id") acknowledges the gap but not the multi-credential case — the sync payload needs a disambiguator (external account id / credential id) or the handler should reject when more than one match exists.

**`refreshOAuthTokens.ts:3`** — `refreshFunction: () => any` erases all type information and is the direct reason issues #1 and #10 compile. Make it generic: `<T>(refreshFunction: () => Promise<T>, ...) => Promise<T | Response>`, which forces call sites to narrow.

**`app-credential.ts:25-27`** — three small hardening gaps in one comparison: the env-provided header name isn't `.toLowerCase()`d (Node lowercases incoming headers, and `.env.example` only *asks* users to use lowercase); the secret comparison isn't constant-time (`crypto.timingSafeEqual`); and if `CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET` is unset, `undefined !== undefined` is `false` and the check passes (mitigated only if `APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED` already requires it — verify in `packages/lib/constants.ts`).

**`decodeOAuthState.ts:9`** — `JSON.parse(req.query.state)` with no `try/catch`; a hand-crafted callback URL yields a 500 instead of a clean redirect. Now higher-blast-radius since `createOAuthAppCredential` depends on it.

**`app-credential.ts:57-59`** — decrypted keys are stored as-is with no validation against the app's key schema; a malformed sync payload silently poisons the credential and only fails later at use time.

**`zoho-bigin/api/add.ts:17`** — the redirect URI was changed from `${appConfig.slug}` to a hardcoded `zoho-bigin` while line 12 still uses `appConfig.slug`. Unrelated to the PR's intent, a DRY regression, and it leaves a template literal with no interpolation. Revert.

**`createOAuthAppCredential.ts`** — `select: { id: true, members: {...} }` selects data never used; `import { decodeOAuthState } from "../oauth/decodeOAuthState"` should be `./decodeOAuthState`; `throw new Error("User does not belong to the team")` should be `HttpError({statusCode: 403})` to match line 25; no dedupe means re-running team OAuth stacks duplicate credentials.
**`app-credential.ts:2,16`** — `import z from "zod"` (default) instead of `import { z }`, and an empty `/** */` JSDoc block above the handler.

**Documentation** — `.env.example` explains the variables but nothing documents the contract self-hosters must implement: the sync endpoint's expected request (`calcomUserId`, `appSlug`, form-encoded) and response shape, or the webhook's encryption format. That contract is currently only discoverable by reading `refreshOAuthTokens.ts`.

goldens.comment: The parseRefreshTokenResponse function incorrectly sets refresh_token to the hardcoded string 'refresh_token' when it's missing from the OAuth refresh token response. This invalidates the token, breaking subsequent token refreshes and causing authentication failures.

The Zod schema in parseRefreshTokenResponse uses computed property keys [z.string().toString()] and [z.string().optional().toString()] in minimumTokenResponseSchema, which is invalid Zod syntax and will throw a runtime error.

parseRefreshTokenResponse returns a Zod safeParse result ({ success, data, error }), not the credential key object. Persisting that as key stores the wrapper instead of the token payload; we should store the parsed data or use schema parse.

When APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED and CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT are set, the refreshFunction helper returns the fetch Response, but several callers (for example GoogleCalendarService.refreshAccessToken expecting res.data, and HubspotCalendarService.refreshAccessToken expecting a HubspotToken) assume it returns the integration-specific token object. That mismatch will cause runtime errors in the sync-enabled path unless the return type or those call sites are adjusted.

When the sync endpoint path is used, res is a fetch Response and has no .data; res?.data will be undefined and token.access_token will throw at runtime. This relies on a consistent return shape from refreshOAuthTokens, which isn’t guaranteed currently.

The `refreshOAuthTokens` function is passed `credentialId` instead of `userId`, which breaks the credential sync functionality by causing incorrect user lookups. This issue can lead to failures in syncing user credentials, impacting user experience.

The Salesforce integration checks `response.statusText` instead of `response.ok` when handling OAuth token refresh responses. This can lead to unreliable behavior, as a successful response may not be correctly identified, resulting in the use of stale credentials and potential authentication failures.

The `jsforce.Connection` is created using stale `credentialKey.access_token` and `credentialKey.instance_url` after a token refresh, which can lead to authentication failures and incorrect data access. Ensure that the connection is established using the refreshed token values instead.

The `appCredentialWebhookRequestBodySchema.parse` function can throw on invalid payloads, resulting in 500 Internal Server Errors instead of the expected 400 Bad Request responses. This can lead to confusion for clients and hinder proper error handling.

adjudication.rationale: Yes. In `minimumTokenResponseSchema`, the computed keys use `z.string().toString()` and `z.string().optional().toString()`. Those are Zod schema objects, and their `.toString()` at runtime yields the same string (typically `"[object Object]"`), so the second computed property overwrites the first in the object literal. That means the schema is effectively `{ access_token: z.string(), "[object Object]": z.unknown().optional() }`, not “any numeric expiry field plus other properties”. Also, `z.object(...)` strips unknown keys by default, so when this schema is used (when credential sharing + sync endpoint are enabled), fields like `expiry_date`, `expires_in`, and `refresh_token` are discarded. This is a concrete correctness bug introduced in the diff and will affect calls like `parseRefreshTokenResponse(responseJson, refreshTokenResponseSchema)` and `parseRefreshTokenResponse(googleCredentials, googleCredentialSchema)` under that feature flag.

A `GET` reaches `schema.parse(undefined)`; a malformed body, a wrong encryption key, or non-JSON plaintext throws out of `symmetricDecrypt`/`JSON.parse`. All of these surface as unhandled 500s (with stack traces in non-production) rather than 400s. Add a method guard and wrap parse/decrypt in `safeParse` + `try/catch` returning 400.
matched_golden_ids: The `appCredentialWebhookRequestBodySchema.parse` function can throw on invalid payloads, resulting in 500 Internal Server Errors instead of the expected 400 Bad Request responses. This can lead to confusion for clients and hinder proper error handling.
adjudication_records.primary_judge_reasoning: The candidate flags that `schema.parse` (and related decrypt/JSON.parse steps) can throw on invalid or missing request bodies, leading to unhandled 500 responses instead of returning a 400 Bad Request. This is the same core issue as the golden comment, though the candidate adds extra context (GET/method guard, decrypt errors).

adjudication_records.issue_text: `apps/web/pages/api/webhook/app-credential.ts:73-80` writes only `key`. Cal.com marks credentials `invalid: true` on `invalid_grant` (see `googlecalendar/lib/CalendarService.ts:108-113`), and invalid credentials are filtered out of calendar lookups. So the sync push that is supposed to *repair* a broken credential leaves it disabled. Add `invalid: false` to the update payload.

adjudication.rationale: The diff does show that `apps/web/pages/api/webhook/app-credential.ts` updates an existing credential by only writing `{ key: keys }` and does not touch any `invalid` field. However, the finding’s core claim—that Cal.com sets `credential.invalid = true` on `invalid_grant` and that invalid credentials are filtered from calendar lookups—is not verifiable from the provided diff. The diff snippet does not show any `invalid` field in the Prisma model usage, any code that sets it, nor any code that filters on it. Therefore the impact (“sync push won’t re-enable a broken credential”) depends on behavior outside what’s shown here.

adjudication_records.issue_text: `apps/web/pages/api/webhook/app-credential.ts:62-70` uses `findFirst` on `(userId, appId)` with no ordering. A user with two Google Calendar accounts gets one of them overwritten at random with the other's keys. The comment ("Can't use prisma upsert as we don't know the id") acknowledges the gap but not the multi-credential case — the sync payload needs a disambiguator (external account id / credential id) or the handler should reject when more than one match exists.

adjudication.rationale: In the new webhook handler, the credential lookup is `prisma.credential.findFirst({ where: { userId: reqBody.userId, appId: appMetadata.slug } })` with no `orderBy` and no uniqueness guarantee in the code path. Using `findFirst` here implicitly assumes there is at most one matching credential; if the database can contain multiple credentials for the same `(userId, appId)` (which is plausible given they did not use `findUnique` and explicitly say they "can't use upsert"), Prisma/DB will return an arbitrary matching row. The subsequent `update` then overwrites whichever credential was returned, potentially corrupting the wrong one. The finding’s recommendation to disambiguate (e.g., include a credential identifier / external account id) or reject when multiple exist follows directly from this behavior.

adjudication_records.issue_text: **`refreshOAuthTokens.ts:3`** — `refreshFunction: () => any` erases all type information and is the direct reason issues #1 and #10 compile. Make it generic: `<T>(refreshFunction: () => Promise<T>, ...) => Promise<T | Response>`, which forces call sites to narrow.

adjudication.rationale:
Yes. In `packages/app-store/_utils/oauth/refreshOAuthTokens.ts`, `refreshFunction: () => any` (and the inferred `any` return type) erases the fact that this helper can return two fundamentally different shapes: (1) a `Response` from `fetch(process.env.CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT, ...)` when syncing is enabled, or (2) whatever the integration-specific refresh function returns.

Because it returns `any`, call sites compile even when they assume a specific token-object type. Example in the diff: `packages/app-store/hubspot/lib/CalendarService.ts` assigns the result to `HubspotToken`: `const hubspotRefreshToken: HubspotToken = await refreshOAuthTokens(...)`. If credential sync is enabled, `refreshOAuthTokens` returns a `Response`, not a `HubspotToken`, so subsequent property access on `hubspotRefreshToken` will be wrong at runtime. A generic/union return type would force callers to narrow/handle the `Response` case instead of compiling unsafely.

adjudication_records.issue_text: **`app-credential.ts:25-27`** — three small hardening gaps in one comparison: the env-provided header name isn't `.toLowerCase()`d (Node lowercases incoming headers, and `.env.example` only *asks* users to use lowercase); the secret comparison isn't constant-time (`crypto.timingSafeEqual`); and if `CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET` is unset, `undefined !== undefined` is `false` and the check passes (mitigated only if `APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED` already requires it — verify in `packages/lib/constants.ts`).

adjudication.rationale: In `apps/web/pages/api/webhook/app-credential.ts`, the webhook auth check is `req.headers[process.env.CALCOM_WEBHOOK_HEADER_NAME || "calcom-webhook-secret"] !== process.env.CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET`. This has a verifiable bypass if `CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET` is unset: when the header lookup yields `undefined` (e.g., header not provided or header name mismatch), the comparison becomes `undefined !== undefined` which is `false`, so the request is accepted. That is a real security/correctness issue introduced by the diff (assuming the feature flag can be enabled without also requiring the secret). Additionally, Node/Next lowercases incoming header keys, so not lowercasing the env-provided header name can make the lookup fail if the env value contains uppercase characters (the `.env.example` comment only suggests lowercase; it’s not enforced). The constant-time comparison point is a hardening suggestion rather than a functional bug, but the unset-secret acceptance is a concrete defect in the code shown.

adjudication_records.issue_text: **`decodeOAuthState.ts:9`** — `JSON.parse(req.query.state)` with no `try/catch`; a hand-crafted callback URL yields a 500 instead of a clean redirect. Now higher-blast-radius since `createOAuthAppCredential` depends on it.

adjudication.rationale: The diff for `packages/app-store/_utils/oauth/decodeOAuthState.ts` only shows an import path change (`../types` -> `../../types`). It does not show any `JSON.parse(req.query.state)` call or lack of try/catch, so the claim is not verifiable from the provided diff. Also, `createOAuthAppCredential` already depended on `decodeOAuthState` before (it was just renamed/moved), so the "higher blast-radius" part is not a new diff-introduced issue.

adjudication_records.issue_text: **`app-credential.ts:57-59`** — decrypted keys are stored as-is with no validation against the app's key schema; a malformed sync payload silently poisons the credential and only fails later at use time.

adjudication.rationale: In `apps/web/pages/api/webhook/app-credential.ts`, the handler decrypts `reqBody.keys` and immediately does `JSON.parse(...)` and then persists the resulting `keys` object into `prisma.credential.update/create` without any validation against an app-specific credential/key schema. Since `appMetadata` is fetched but not used to validate the shape of `keys`, any payload that decrypts to valid JSON but has an unexpected structure will be accepted and stored, potentially breaking later code paths that assume a specific credential shape. (Only invalid JSON would fail immediately via `JSON.parse`, but malformed-yet-valid JSON would be stored “as-is”.)

adjudication_records.issue_text: **Documentation** — `.env.example` explains the variables but nothing documents the contract self-hosters must implement: the sync endpoint's expected request (`calcomUserId`, `appSlug`, form-encoded) and response shape, or the webhook's encryption format. That contract is currently only discoverable by reading `refreshOAuthTokens.ts`.

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds new self-hosting env vars (CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT, CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET, CALCOM_WEBHOOK_HEADER_NAME, CALCOM_APP_CREDENTIAL_ENCRYPTION_KEY) and introduces implicit integration contracts in code. In `refreshOAuthTokens.ts`, the sync endpoint is called with a POST body of `new URLSearchParams({ calcomUserId, appSlug })` (form-encoded) and comments indicate the response should contain only access token + expiry. None of that request/response shape is documented in `.env.example` (it only lists the variables, with no contract details). Similarly, the webhook handler expects `keys` to be an AES256-encrypted JSON string decrypted with `CALCOM_APP_CREDENTIAL_ENCRYPTION_KEY`, but `.env.example` does not document the webhook payload/encryption format beyond a brief note. So the contract is indeed only discoverable by reading the new code.
